source.title: Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages
source.authors: Abhinav Menon; Manish Shrivastava; David Krueger; E. Lubana

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some internal section references appear as 'Sec. ??', and some plotted material is flattened, but the relevant results are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE-identified features are robustly identifiable and causally relevant, and finds that feature identification depends on training settings and that ordinary SAE features can be correlational without the expected causal effect.
record.gate_note: The study does not test superposition geometry, feature capacity, or polysemanticity. Reconstruction-accuracy values and SAE scaling results are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions. Rows record feature correlations, feature interventions, sensitivity statements, and interventions on SAEs trained with causal regularization.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on small Transformers trained on formal languages. It reports that feature identification depends on regularizer and normalization, and that well-correlated SAE features have no causal effect when clamped. Both results bear on whether SAE features are stable units of the model's own computation (V5). The models are not LLMs, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find SAEs readily yield latents correlated with generative variables, but identification is highly sensitive to the training pipeline. Identified latents rarely have causal impact on the model. A causal-loss SAE gives task-specific causal features, which the authors call a proof of concept with its own inductive bias (MLP-read features only).
record.recipe_differences: Does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method. It trains SAEs on hidden activations of small Transformers trained on synthetic formal languages, then studies feature correlations, interventions, and a modified causal loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature identification varies with normalization, regularization, and other training settings. The authors report L1-regularized SAEs consistently fail to find interpretable features, while top-k SAEs identify features across the languages. Causal regularization yields causal features for selected English parts of speech but not for Dyck-2 or Expr.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The experiments use simplified synthetic formal-language models rather than real LLMs. Feature identification is manual and correlational; the paper does not establish completeness or canonical status. Many intervention results are presented in figures without numeric values, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The text also has some missing section references and flattened figure material.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant result rows were omitted. Reconstruction-accuracy and reconstruction-scaling results were not included because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Completeness of the SAE dictionary, and whether features match across seeds or dictionary sizes, are not tested.
Not tested: no toy superposition geometry or sparsity-dependent transition.
Not tested: no neuron polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
Not tested: small formal-language Transformers only, not LLMs. The interpretable latents (R1-R11) are recovered in toy models.
Not tested: feature dimensionality is not examined.

missing.what: Reconstruction accuracy (% valid generations) per regularizer × normalization variant. It ranges from ~0% to 99.88% with no consistent trend across languages. This is the quantitative basis for the instability claim.
Causal-loss SAEs find interpretable features only for adjectives, verbs and adverbs (MLP-read), and none in the Dyck-2 or Expr models. Which features are found depends on the training objective.

record.verdict_notes: R1-R11 are correlation scores for hand-picked latents. They are kept at V5 cannot_determine because they do not speak to completeness, stability or canonicity. The subjects are toy 2-layer, 128-d Transformers on PCFGs, so V4 (LLMs) is not addressed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features outnumbering dimensions, overlap, near-orthogonality, or a sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or competition for limited representational capacity.
Does not study polysemantic neurons or whether they arise without capacity pressure.
The studied models are small Transformers trained on synthetic formal languages, not real LLMs; the study does not test feature distribution across neurons in LLMs.
Tests feature identifiability sensitivity and causal effects, but does not establish whether SAE features are complete or canonical units of the model's representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of underlying features.

relationships.condition: Ordinary (non-causal-loss) SAE features on Expr counter and English part-of-speech, clamped across [-vmax, vmax]
relationships.reason: Features correlate with explanations at r=0.93-0.999, yet clamping them changes nothing in generations (R2, R12, R13). They are not causally used units of the model.
relationships.display_finding: Features correlated with their explanations at r = 0.93–0.999, yet clamping them across the full range left generations unchanged, so they are not units the model uses causally.
